hints: Number the ring to give the two ethyl substituents the lowest possible locants and look at their relative positions on E compared to D.
walkthrough:
Read the substitution pattern**
Look at E beside D. D has the two $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ groups on adjacent carbons, that is 1,2. In E one ethyl group has moved so there is one unsubstituted carbon between them. Counting around the ring the shortest way gives positions 1 and 3.

hints: Think about what would happen if the solvent itself contained $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms and gave huge peaks that hide the sample peaks.
walkthrough:
Why a special solvent is needed**
In $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR every proton in the tube gives a signal. If you dissolve your hydrocarbon in ordinary $\text{CHCl}_{3}$ or water, the solvent protons would swamp the spectrum. You need a solvent with no $^{1}\text{H}$, so deuterium $^{2}\text{H}$ is used because it resonates at a different frequency. The standard choice is $\text{CDCl}_{3}$.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ (deuterated chloroform / $\text{CCl}_{4}$ or other solvent with no protons)

hints: Recall which types of proton disappear after shaking with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ and check whether E contains any of those groups.
walkthrough:
Link D2O to exchangeable protons**
Shaking with $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ only changes the spectrum if there is an $\text{O-H}$, $\text{N-H}$ or similar acidic proton that can swap: $\text{R-OH} + \text{D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-OD} + \text{HOD}$. The $\text{R-OD}$ peak does not appear in $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR, so that signal vanishes. E is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3})_{2}$, containing only $\text{C-H}$ protons on alkyl groups and the aromatic ring. None of these exchange, so both spectra are identical.
Final answer: No difference between the two spectra, as E is a hydrocarbon with no labile $\text{O-H}$ or $\text{N-H}$ protons that can exchange with D.

hints: Use Table 7.2 to match $\delta$ 1.3 and 2.7 to alkyl protons and $\delta$ 7.1 to aromatic protons, then count equivalent protons in 1,2-diethylbenzene.
Remember the two ethyl groups in D are equivalent, so add the protons from both $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups together and both $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups together.
Apply the n+1 rule to the $\text{CH}_{3}\text{-CH}_{2}$ fragment to predict triplet versus quartet splitting.
walkthrough:
Assign the aromatic peak**
The singlet-like peak at $\delta$ 7.1 falls in the 6.0 to 9.0 range for $\text{H-Ar}$ in Table 7.2. D has formula $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ with 4 ring protons left after disubstitution, so integration is 4H.

Assign the alkyl peaks by shift and integration**
$\delta$ 1.3 is in the 0.9 to 1.7 alkane region, typical for $\text{CH}_{3}$ away from the ring. There are two equivalent $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups, so $3 + 3 = 6\text{H}$. $\delta$ 2.7 is in the 2.3 to 3.0 region for alkyl next to aromatic ring, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{-Ar}$. There are two equivalent $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups, so $2 + 2 = 4\text{H}$. The ratio 6:4:4 adds to 14H, matching $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$.

Explain the splitting with n+1**
The $\text{CH}_{3}$ protons see 2 neighbouring protons on the adjacent $\text{CH}_{2}$, so $n+1 = 2+1 = 3$, a triplet. The $\text{CH}_{2}$ protons see 3 neighbouring protons on the adjacent $\text{CH}_{3}$, so $n+1 = 3+1 = 4$, a quartet. That is exactly what Fig. 7.2 shows at 1.3 and 2.7 ppm.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.3: 6 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms, $\text{CH}_{3}$, triplet; $\delta$ 2.7: 4 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms, $\text{CH}_{2}$ next to Ar, quartet; $\delta$ 7.1: 4 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms (aromatic $\text{H-Ar}$).

hints: Count equivalent carbons by looking for a mirror plane that swaps the two identical ethyl groups in the 1,2 and 1,3 isomers.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbons from symmetry**
In D, 1,2-diethylbenzene, the two ethyl groups are equivalent. The ring gives 3 unique aromatic carbons ($\text{C1/C2}$, $\text{C3/C6}$, $\text{C4/C5}$) plus one $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbon type and one $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbon type, total 5. In E, 1,3-diethylbenzene, the symmetry is lower. The ring gives 4 unique aromatic carbons ($\text{C1/C3}$, $\text{C2}$, $\text{C4/C6}$, $\text{C5}$) plus one $\text{CH}_{2}$ type and one $\text{CH}_{3}$ type, total 6. Different numbers of peaks therefore distinguish them even though proton NMR looks very similar.
Final answer: The carbon-13 NMR spectrum of D has 5 peaks. The carbon-13 NMR spectrum of E has 6 peaks.

hints: Write the molecular formulae first: D is $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ and F (phthalic acid) is $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{4}$, then balance C with $\text{CO}_{2}$ and H with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ before finding [O].
walkthrough:
Balance atoms using [O]**
D is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5})_{2} = \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$. F is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{COOH})_{2} = \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{4}$. Each ethyl side chain loses one carbon as $\text{CO}_{2}$, so 2 $\text{CO}_{2}$ are needed for carbon balance: $10 = 8 + 2$. Hydrogen: $14 = 6 + 2 \times 4$, so $4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ are needed. Oxygen: right side has $4 + 4 + 4 = 12$ O atoms, so 12[O] are needed on the left. This gives $$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14} + 12[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{4} + 2\text{CO}_{2} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Recall what $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ does to each $\text{-COOH}$ group and work out the structure of G from $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{2}$.
Think about how one molecule of ethane-1,2-diol can react twice with the two $\text{-COCl}$ groups of the same G molecule to close a ring for J.

For K with formula $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{12}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{6}$, count atoms to see it must contain two benzene rings joined by one diol bridge with one $\text{-COCl}$ left unreacted on each ring.
walkthrough:
Form G, the diacyl chloride**
Carboxylic acids react with excess $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ to give acyl chlorides: $\text{R-COOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{R-COCl} + \text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$. Both $\text{-COOH}$ groups on F react, keeping the 1,2 positions on the ring. So G is $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{COCl})_{2}$$ with the two $\text{-COCl}$ groups ortho to each other.

Close the ring to make J**
Acyl chlorides react with alcohols to give esters. One $\text{HOCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ molecule provides two $\text{-OH}$ groups that can react with the two $\text{-COCl}$ groups of the same G molecule, losing $2\text{HCl}$. This forms a cyclic diester: the benzene ring with $\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-}$ looping across the 1,2 positions. Formula check: $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{2} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2} - 2\text{HCl} = \text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{4}$, which is J.

Link two rings to make K**
If instead each $\text{-OH}$ of the diol reacts with a different G molecule, and only one $\text{-COCl}$ on each G reacts, you get an open chain dimer. The centre is $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-}$ joining two phthaloyl units, each still carrying one unreacted $\text{-COCl}$. That is $$\text{Cl-C(=O)-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-C(=O)-Cl}$$ Formula check: $2 \times \text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{2} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{2} - 2\text{HCl} = \text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{12}\text{Cl}_{2}\text{O}_{6}$, which is K.

Final answer: G: 1,2-$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}(\text{COCl})_{2}$, benzene-1,2-dicarbonyl dichloride. J: cyclic diester where $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-}$ bridges the 1,2 positions of the same ring, $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{4}$. K: $\text{ClOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COCl}$, two 1,2-disubstituted rings linked by one $\text{-COO-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-OOC-}$ bridge with terminal $\text{-COCl}$ groups.
